---
title: "Suggested reading"
---

Several books and reviews have shaped how I think about the questions in this course. I have collected them here, together with the papers behind our examples and references for when a calculation or a piece of code is unfamiliar. This is a collection to return to when a question interests you. All of the reading is suggested; we will develop the ideas we need together in class.

**What should this page help you do?** Find a fuller explanation of an idea, trace a claim back to the study that made it, and compare the evidence in that study with the conclusion you want to draw. If a result seems surprising, following the reference should let you ask what was actually measured. There is no reading list to finish before you can take part.

## On Exactitude in Science {#borges}

Jorge Luis Borges's *On Exactitude in Science* (1946) is a short story about taking completeness too far. We use it when asking what a model should retain for a particular purpose. Andrew Hurley's English translation is reproduced in [Box 2 of *The Human Cell Atlas*](https://elifesciences.org/articles/27041).

## Two introductions to machine learning {#introductory-reviews}

For an introduction to machine learning in chemistry, I still recommend our review: Kevin Maik Jablonka, Daniele Ongari, Seyed Mohamad Moosavi, and Berend Smit (2020), [*Big-Data Science in Porous Materials: Materials Genomics and Machine Learning*](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.chemrev.0c00004), *Chemical Reviews* 120, 8066–8129. Porous materials give us concrete examples, but many of the questions arise elsewhere in chemistry. Which observations should a model learn from? How do we describe a material to a computer? How do we evaluate what it has learned? The first part develops these ideas; the second examines applications, including gas storage and separation, stability, and synthesis. The review is open access, with another [full-text copy at PubMed Central](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7453404/).

I also recommend Pankaj Mehta et al. (2019), [*A high-bias, low-variance introduction to Machine Learning for physicists*](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.physrep.2019.03.001), *Physics Reports* 810, 1–124. Why can a model fit the observations we give it and still predict new ones poorly? The review develops the statistical ideas behind that question before moving to more elaborate methods, drawing connections to statistical physics along the way. Its [free arXiv version](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.08823) first appeared in 2018 and was revised in 2019. The mathematics becomes more demanding as the discussion develops; we will work through the foundations together. The accompanying Python notebooks provide further examples, although they have not been tested in our course environment.

Both are substantial reviews to return to as questions arise. There is no need to finish either before the first class.

## Books I recommend {#core-books}

Moritz Hardt and Benjamin Recht's [*Patterns, Predictions, and Actions: Foundations of Machine Learning*](https://mlstory.org/) (Princeton University Press, 2022) is a particularly useful companion to this course. It connects the mathematics of learning to the questions of what we predict and what we do with a prediction. Its distinction between a sample and a population is central to our discussion of test error. The authors provide a free web edition, whose wording and pagination differ from the print book. Later mathematical arguments use probability, calculus, and linear algebra.

Kate Crawford's [*Atlas of AI: Power, Politics, and the Planetary Costs of Artificial Intelligence*](https://yalebooks.yale.edu/book/9780300264630/atlas-of-ai/) (Yale University Press, 2021; paperback 2022) matters to me because the model is only part of the story. Data, labour, resources, and power are part of it too. I discuss that connection [below](#atlas-of-ai).

Carissa Véliz's [*Prophecy: Prediction, Power, and the Fight for the Future, from Ancient Oracles to AI*](https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/759692/prophecy-by-carissa-veliz/9780385550970/) (Doubleday, 2026; UK edition, Swift Press) places our current enthusiasm for prediction in a longer history. It raises a question that also matters in the laboratory: [what happens when people act on a prediction?](#prophecy)

Dan Davies's [*The Unaccountability Machine*](https://profilebooks.com/work/the-unaccountability-machine/) (Profile Books, 2024) brings cybernetics into a discussion of organisations and responsibility. It helps us ask [who can question and change a decision](#unaccountability-machine) when it is attributed to a system.

For the calculations inside neural networks, I recommend Simon J. D. Prince's [*Understanding Deep Learning*](https://udlbook.github.io/udlbook/) (MIT Press, 2023). Its diagrams, equations, and examples give us several ways to examine the same operation. The author provides a free edition and Python notebooks; I have noted the connections to our examples [below](#understanding-deep-learning).

## Writing code {#practical-references}

Philippe Schwaller's group provides [*Practical Programming for Chemistry*](https://schwallergroup.github.io/practical-programming-in-chemistry/), with explanations of [Jupyter notebooks](https://schwallergroup.github.io/practical-programming-in-chemistry/tutorials/lecture_02/01_jupyter_notebooks.html), [variables, types, and other Python basics](https://schwallergroup.github.io/practical-programming-in-chemistry/tutorials/lecture_02/02_python_basics.html). The Python explanations are useful when the chemistry makes sense but the code does not yet. That course uses Jupyter; we use marimo, so the notebook controls differ. Our [setup instructions](setup.qmd) describe the environment used in this course.

Andrew D. White's [*Deep Learning for Molecules & Materials*](https://dmol.pub/) connects mathematical models to molecular examples and code. The chapter on [regression and model assessment](https://dmol.pub/ml/regression.html) covers several of the questions raised by our calibration experiment. It is freely available online; later chapters assume more Python and mathematics.

## The tools around Python {#computing-tools}

Programming courses often begin as though everybody already knows what a shell is, where a command should be typed, and what happens when it runs. Anish Athalye, Jon Gjengset, and Jose Javier Gonzalez Ortiz's [*The Missing Semester of Your CS Education*](https://missing.csail.mit.edu/) addresses much of that assumed knowledge.

The 2026 [introduction to the shell](https://missing.csail.mit.edu/2026/course-shell/) explains what the shell does and how to navigate with commands such as `pwd`, `ls`, and `cd`. These are the same ideas used in our [computing basics](setup.qmd#computing-basics). Windows users can follow the Unix-shell examples in [Ubuntu through WSL 2](setup.qmd#windows-wsl). The notes and recordings are free.

Its chapter on [development environments and tools](https://missing.csail.mit.edu/2026/development-environment/) explains editors and integrated development environments. Python's own tutorial explains [virtual environments in section 12.1](https://docs.python.org/3.12/tutorial/venv.html#introduction). The distinction is useful: the editor is where we work on the code; the Python environment determines which interpreter and packages run it.

## AI and scientific understanding {#lecture-1}

Hardt and Recht's [**Prediction and action**](https://mlstory.org/introduction.html#prediction-and-action) connects the broad ambition of AI to the consequences of a particular use. Predicting what will happen and deciding what to do are related problems, but a good answer to the first does not settle the second.

Hanchen Wang et al. (2023), [*Scientific discovery in the age of artificial intelligence*](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-06221-2), *Nature* 620, 47–60, reviews applications across scientific work. Lisa Messeri and M. J. Crockett (2024), [*Artificial intelligence and illusions of understanding in scientific research*](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-07146-0), *Nature* 627, 49–58, asks how adopting these tools might change what researchers believe they understand and which questions they pursue. Read together, they bring out a tension in the opening lecture: a tool can expand what we can do while narrowing what we think to ask. Wang and colleagues review applications; Messeri and Crockett develop a conceptual argument about possible consequences. Full articles may require institutional access.

For materials chemistry, Seyed Mohamad Moosavi, Kevin Maik Jablonka, and Berend Smit (2020), [*The Role of Machine Learning in the Understanding and Design of Materials*](https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.0c09105), *JACS* 142, 20273–20287, considers the relationship between prediction, understanding, and design. The Introduction connects these questions to the problems materials researchers want to solve. The paper is open access.


## What do we mean by probability? {#probability-lenses}

The distinction between Bayesian and frequentist inference becomes easier to discuss when we say what the probability concerns. Is it uncertainty about a parameter, given a model and observations? Or the behaviour of a procedure if we repeatedly collected data?

Stanford's *STATS 200: Introduction to Statistical Inference* (Autumn 2016), [Lecture 20, **Bayesian analysis**](https://web.stanford.edu/class/stats200/Lecture20.pdf), introduces prior and posterior distributions in section 20.1. [Lecture 18, **Confidence intervals**](https://web.stanford.edu/class/stats200/Lecture18.pdf), explains the repeated-sampling interpretation of a confidence interval. Both PDFs are freely available. The opening explanations are useful even before working through the derivations.

Both approaches require assumptions. A neural-network architecture alone tells us neither how uncertainty has been represented nor what a reported probability means. We will need that distinction when uncertainty helps us choose the next experiment.

## What does a benchmark score stand for? {#science-and-commercial-claims}

Adrian Mirza et al. (2025), [*A framework for evaluating the chemical knowledge and reasoning abilities of large language models against the expertise of chemists*](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41557-025-01815-x), *Nature Chemistry* 17, 1027–1034, introduces ChemBench. 

Read it alongside [TakeoverBench's ChemBench page](https://takeoverbench.com/benchmarks/chem_bench), which places the benchmark under “Chemical weapons development” (accessed 27 October 2026). Its **Why this benchmark?** paragraph gives the selection rationale; its [About page](https://takeoverbench.com/about) explains the initiative's purpose. The [lecture discussion](lectures/01-ai-and-science.qmd#science-and-model-claims) asks what evidence would connect the question-answering score to that broader capability. Identifying a gap in that argument does not, on its own, establish the presence or absence of the risk.


## Atlas of AI {#atlas-of-ai}

A model arrives in our notebook as a file or an API call. It is easy to begin the story there. Crawford's *Atlas of AI* asks us to look at what had to happen before that point: extracting resources, building infrastructure, doing work, collecting data, and deciding how the world should be classified. This is why I consider it an essential book for thinking about AI, including AI in science.

In chemistry, a table of measurements can make a great deal of human work disappear from view. Someone synthesised the materials, maintained the instrument, decided which results were usable, and recorded them. Someone else may have assembled the table. The chapters **Labor** and **Data** give us reasons to pay attention to that work. **Classification** connects to our question about what happens when a solubility measurement becomes a yes/no label. **Earth** and **Power** extend the discussion to resources and the institutions that control them.


## Prophecy {#prophecy}

Our interest in predicting the future is much older than machine learning. Carissa Véliz's [*Prophecy* (2026)](https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/759692/prophecy-by-carissa-veliz/9780385550970/) places contemporary predictive technologies within that longer history and examines how predictions gain authority and shape people's choices. The publisher offers a sample; the full book requires a library copy or purchase.

For our course, consider a laboratory that uses predicted stability to decide which materials to synthesise. The ranking helps determine where time and resources go. The resulting measurements may then enter the next training dataset. A candidate that was never tested remains unknown, even if the model gave it a low score. The prediction has helped shape the evidence available to its successor.

This laboratory example is our own way of bringing the question back to chemistry. It also connects to Hardt and Recht's [**Prediction and action**](https://mlstory.org/introduction.html#prediction-and-action): predictive accuracy, the consequences of acting on a prediction, and the authority to make that decision each need attention.

## The Unaccountability Machine {#unaccountability-machine}

Dan Davies's [*The Unaccountability Machine: Why Big Systems Make Terrible Decisions—and How the World Lost Its Mind*](https://profilebooks.com/work/the-unaccountability-machine/) (Profile Books, 2024) is a useful companion to the cybernetics discussion. Through Stafford Beer's work on management cybernetics, it examines how organisations process information and make decisions. Davies describes *accountability sinks*: arrangements in which responsibility becomes difficult to locate because decisions have been delegated to procedures or systems.

For this course, I would bring that question back to the laboratory. Suppose a screening model excludes a material from further experiments. Who can question that exclusion? Where would evidence that the model missed something go, and who could act on it? Explaining the calculation would answer only part of that problem.

Chapters 2, **Stafford Beer**, and 5, **Cybernetics Without Diagrams**, are relevant places to explore this connection. The [US publisher lists the contents](https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/U/bo252799883.html); that edition appeared in 2025. Profile Books offers a preview; the full book requires a library copy or purchase. Wiener's [original account](#historical-sources) provides the earlier formulation of cybernetics, while Davies follows its implications for organisational decisions.

## Prediction, explanation, and causality {#claims-and-evidence}

In the reaction example, we can explain exactly how the model uses temperature and still not know what would happen if we turned up the heater. Hardt and Recht's [Chapter 9, **Causality**](https://mlstory.org/causal.html), develops the distinction between observation and intervention. Its opening discussion connects directly to the example; **Interventions and causal effects** introduces the formal treatment. The web text is free.

Eleanor Dillon, Jacob LaRiviere, Scott Lundberg, Jonathan Roth, and Vasilis Syrgkanis work through a related problem in the SHAP documentation: [**Be careful when interpreting predictive models in search of causal insights**](https://shap.readthedocs.io/en/latest/example_notebooks/overviews/Be%20careful%20when%20interpreting%20predictive%20models%20in%20search%20of%20causal%20insights.html). Their example shows why a feature-importance plot can describe a fitted predictor without justifying an intervention. The prepared output can be read without installing SHAP.

Galit Shmueli (2010), [*To Explain or to Predict?*](https://doi.org/10.1214/10-STS330), *Statistical Science* 25, 289–310, examines how these different purposes change modelling. Here, “explanatory modelling” concerns causal explanation; it differs from explaining the output of a fitted model.

## Learning from a finite dataset {#lecture-2}

Hardt and Recht's [**Sample versus population**](https://mlstory.org/supervised.html#sample-versus-population), in Chapter 3, provides the distinction behind our calibration example. We can calculate an error exactly for a finite set of observations while remaining uncertain about the error on future cases. The following **Supervised learning** section puts the fitting problem into notation. Chapter 6's discussion of the [generalisation gap and model complexity](https://mlstory.org/generalization.html) develops the question raised by our increasingly flexible polynomial curves.

The scikit-learn developers' [**Common pitfalls and recommended practices**](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/common_pitfalls.html) makes two practical problems concrete: **Inconsistent preprocessing** and **Data leakage**. Its paired code examples show how information can enter model development through a transformation applied before fitting the model itself.

The [two introductory reviews](#introductory-reviews) also develop these questions. Mehta et al. explain how fitting the available observations can fail to produce useful predictions for new ones. Section 7 of Jablonka, Ongari, Moosavi, and Smit's *Big-Data Science in Porous Materials* discusses model evaluation and comparison in materials chemistry.

## Learning from a collection of materials (biased collection) {#molsim}

The [MOF practical](lectures/03-mof-uptake.qmd) adapts my [MolSim 2024 notebook](https://github.com/kjappelbaum/ml_molsim/blob/0ebed176b972c9ba9ddf7b6e3a4d04eaf3f32409/molsim_ml.ipynb). The original contains further exercises on descriptors, hyperparameters, and model inspection, with code left for students to complete. The course kit supplies the working notebook and data for our class.

My [MolSim 2023 lecture slides](https://www.compchem.nl/wp-content/uploads/molsim2023/L09_Machine-Learning.pdf) develop the explanations behind those calculations, with contributions credited to Mohamad Moosavi. They ask where ML enters a molecular calculation (p. 3), how chemical knowledge restricts the functions we consider (pp. 7–13), what an empirical error measures (p. 23), and how a prediction can be built from similarities to training examples (pp. 53–57). We develop these ideas more slowly in our lecture notes. The slides are an additional reference; the later sections on learned potentials and sampling (pp. 86–92) also connect to the simulation part of the course. Numerical performance claims in that 2023 talk refer to the cited studies and their settings.

Seyed Mohamad Moosavi et al. (2020), [*Understanding the diversity of the metal-organic framework ecosystem*](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-020-17755-8), *Nature Communications* 11, 4068, asks what makes a new structure informative. That question matters when a database contains many related materials.

Kevin Maik Jablonka, Andrew S. Rosen, Aditi S. Krishnapriyan, and Berend Smit (2023), [*An Ecosystem for Digital Reticular Chemistry*](https://doi.org/10.1021/acscentsci.2c01177), *ACS Central Science* 9, 563–581, examines evaluation and the infrastructure around materials models. **Case Study 1: The impact of data leakage**, in the Appendix, shows why distinct rows need not make a genuinely new prediction problem. 

The table itself also deserves attention. Kevin Maik Jablonka, Luc Patiny, and Berend Smit (2022), [*Making the collective knowledge of chemistry open and machine actionable*](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41557-022-00910-7), *Nature Chemistry* 14, 365–376, discusses what is needed for chemical information to be reusable. A number without its units, conditions, and provenance leaves another person or program with considerable guesswork. 

For the optional descriptor-shuffling calculation, scikit-learn's [permutation-importance documentation](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/permutation_importance.html) explains both the operation and its interpretation. It concerns the fitted model's use of the supplied information.

## Understanding Deep Learning {#understanding-deep-learning}

Prince's [*Understanding Deep Learning*](https://udlbook.github.io/udlbook/) is the book I recommend when we want to see what happens inside a network. The small examples make it possible to follow a calculation before handing it to a library. This fits the way we will work: draw the function, calculate an output, change a parameter, and then examine what changes.

## Recognising familiar molecules {#chemical-evaluation}

Izhar Wallach and Abraham Heifets (2018), [*Most Ligand-Based Classification Benchmarks Reward Memorization Rather than Generalization*](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jcim.7b00403), *Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling* 58, 916–932, examines redundancy in ligand-based benchmarks. A [free author preprint](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.06619v2) is available; it is a separate version from the journal article.

A high score is less surprising when the evaluation molecules resemble ones the model has already seen. Whether that resemblance is acceptable depends on what we intend to predict. This study gives a chemical example of why choosing a split is also choosing a question about generalisation.

## The decision about what gets measured {#benchmark-purpose}

Our two calibration models exchange places when we change the error measure. The same issue appears in larger model comparisons: the apparent winner depends on what the comparison rewards.

Mostafa Dehghani et al. (2021), [*The Benchmark Lottery*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.07002), examines how benchmark choices alter the ordering of methods. Its examples span several machine-learning domains. Kawin Ethayarajh and Dan Jurafsky (2020), [*Utility is in the Eye of the User: A Critique of NLP Leaderboards*](https://aclanthology.org/2020.emnlp-main.393/), *EMNLP*, 4846–4853, uses a formal analysis of utility to examine the gap between leaderboard incentives and practical needs. The first is an open preprint; the second is an openly available opinion paper about language-processing benchmarks.

For a laboratory, accuracy might matter alongside cost, turnaround time, or the consequences of a large error. A ranking built around one score leaves those preferences partly unstated. These papers give us ways to examine that choice.

## Molecular models and choosing experiments {#later-topics}

The later practicals connect molecular representations to predictions, generated candidates, and decisions about which experiment to perform. These references develop those connections.

| Topic | Reference | Background and access |
|---|---|---|
| Molecular graphs | White, [**Graph Neural Networks**](https://dmol.pub/dl/gnn.html). Describes how information passes between neighbouring atoms in a molecular graph. | Guided technical chapter; free web text. |
| Predicting molecular energies | White, [**Predicting DFT Energies with GNNs**](https://dmol.pub/applied/QM9.html). Applies graph models to a specified energy-prediction task. | Applied chapter after the graph introduction; free web text. Energy prediction alone does not validate molecular dynamics. |
| Learned potentials | Oliver T. Unke et al. (2021), [**Machine Learning Force Fields**](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.chemrev.0c01111), *Chemical Reviews* 121, 10142–10186. Reviews how fitted potentials are constructed and assessed for molecular simulation. | Detailed review for later consultation; open-access journal article and [author preprint](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.07067). |
| Generative models | White, [**Variational Autoencoder**](https://dmol.pub/dl/VAE.html). Develops the encoder, latent variables, and decoder used to generate candidates. | Technical extension after neural networks; free web text. |
| Choosing experiments | Benjamin J. Shields et al. (2021), [**Bayesian reaction optimization as a tool for chemical synthesis**](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-021-03213-y), *Nature* 590, 89–96. Shows how an objective and an experimental budget enter reaction optimisation. | Chemical research example; full text may require institutional access. |
| LLMs with tools | Andres M. Bran et al. (2024), [**Augmenting large language models with chemistry tools**](https://www.nature.com/articles/s42256-024-00832-8), *Nature Machine Intelligence* 6, 525–535. Describes the contributions of the language model and the external chemistry tools. | Research case study for the LLM session; open-access journal article and [free 2023 preprint](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.05376), with a different title and version from the published article. |

## Examples from our research {#research-examples}

Some of these questions have also shaped our own research. These papers make particular modelling choices visible: the objective, the examples supplied to a model, the representation, and the conversion of a paper into data.

### Choosing among competing objectives {#multiobjective-learning}

Kevin Maik Jablonka, Giriprasad Melpatti Jothiappan, Shefang Wang, Berend Smit, and Brian Yoo (2021), [*Bias free multiobjective active learning for materials design and discovery*](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-021-22437-0), *Nature Communications* 12, 2312; [open university copy](https://escholarship.org/uc/item/9mr3w2s3).

Improving one material property can worsen another. This paper considers learning in the presence of competing objectives. The method can help identify promising trade-offs, but someone still has to decide which properties matter and which compromises are acceptable.

### A language model as a property predictor {#predictive-language-models}

Kevin Maik Jablonka, Philippe Schwaller, Andres Ortega-Guerrero, and Berend Smit (2024), [*Leveraging large language models for predictive chemistry*](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42256-023-00788-1), *Nature Machine Intelligence* 6, 161–169. Open access.

Here, language models are adapted using labelled chemical examples. The **Classification** section makes that learning problem concrete. The procedure differs from asking an ordinary chatbot a chemistry question: the examples, adaptation, and evaluation are part of what produced the reported result.

### Information supplied and information used {#representation-and-model}

Nawaf Alampara, Santiago Miret, and Kevin Maik Jablonka (2026), [*Less can be more for predicting properties with large language models*](https://doi.org/10.1038/s43588-026-01045-2), *Nature Computational Science*, published 12 October 2026. Open access.

A representation can contain information that a particular model fails to use. Figure 1 and the **Representation** subsection separate information about categories from information about coordinates. The tested models and tasks give us a concrete example of the distinction between supplying more detail and making a better prediction.

### Turning a paper into a table {#chemical-data-extraction}

Mara Schilling-Wilhelmi et al. (2025), [*From text to insight: large language models for chemical data extraction*](https://doi.org/10.1039/D4CS00913D), *Chemical Society Reviews* 54, 1125–1150. Open access; first published online in December 2024.

Extracting a value from a paper also means deciding which units, conditions, and source information must travel with it. Section 3, **Structured data extraction workflow**, develops that problem. The [open companion book](https://matextract.pub/) provides worked examples; its code has not been tested in our course environment.

## Sources for the history {#historical-sources}

The original papers and proposals help show what the researchers were trying to achieve, what they could demonstrate, and what remained an ambition.

| Source | Connection to the lecture |
|---|---|
| Alan M. Turing (1948), [**Intelligent Machinery**](https://www.npl.co.uk/getattachment/84156b8e-1b00-45b7-9f5e-3179cfa458c5/80916595-Intelligent-Machinery.pdf?lang=en-US) | An NPL report written before the name artificial intelligence was introduced. The opening summary already discusses intelligent behaviour and teaching machines. Free scan held by NPL; 1948 is the report date. |
| Norbert Wiener (1948), [**Cybernetics: Or Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine**](https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262537841/cybernetics-or-control-and-communication-in-the-animal-and-the-machine/) | The introduction explains the scope of cybernetics. Feedback, control, and communication connect biological and engineered systems. An overlapping tradition, rather than a previous name for exactly the same field. The publisher links an open-access reissue of the expanded 1961 second edition. |
| Alan M. Turing (1950), [**Computing Machinery and Intelligence**](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~frank/csc2501/Readings/R1_Turing/Turing-1950.pdf), *Mind* 59, 433–460 | Sections 1–2 turn a question about thinking into an observable test. Section 7 considers learning machines. Freely accessible university-hosted copy. |
| John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester, and Claude Shannon (1955), [**A Proposal for the Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence**](https://www-formal.stanford.edu/jmc/history/dartmouth/dartmouth.html) | The title uses the name coined by McCarthy. The proposal is dated 31 August 1955; the meeting took place in 1956. Its opening and list of topics show the breadth of the ambition. Free author-hosted text. |
| Frank Rosenblatt (1958), [**The Perceptron: A Probabilistic Model for Information Storage and Organization in the Brain**](https://web.stanford.edu/class/psych209a/ReadingsByDate/01_30/Rosenblatt58Perceptron.pdf), *Psychological Review* 65, 386–408; DOI `10.1037/h0042519` | Opening pages 386–388: the questions and assumptions motivating the model. The simple threshold equation in our notes is a teaching abstraction. Freely accessible university-hosted copy. |
| Bruce G. Buchanan, Georgia L. Sutherland, and Edward A. Feigenbaum (1969), **Heuristic DENDRAL: A Program for Generating Explanatory Hypotheses in Organic Chemistry**, in *Machine Intelligence 4*, 209–254 | A historical chemical example of constrained hypothesis generation. The [Stanford collection record](https://cs.stanford.edu/people/eaf/wordpress/publications/) identifies the chapter and report HPP-68-3; this is a bibliographic record, not a direct full-text link. |
| David E. Rumelhart, Geoffrey E. Hinton, and Ronald J. Williams (1986), [**Learning representations by back-propagating errors**](https://www.nature.com/articles/323533a0), *Nature* 323, 533–536 | Intermediate layers learn representations useful for the task. Full text may require institutional access. |
| Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, and Geoffrey E. Hinton (2012), [**ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks**](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2012/hash/c399862d3b9d6b76c8436e924a68c45b-Abstract.html), *Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems* 25 | A demonstration of deep convolutional networks on an image-classification benchmark. Proceedings page includes the paper. |
| Ashish Vaswani et al. (2017), [**Attention Is All You Need**](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762) | The Transformer architecture, introduced for sequence modelling. Free preprint. |
| John Jumper et al. (2021), [**Highly accurate protein structure prediction with AlphaFold**](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-021-03819-2), *Nature* 596, 583–589; [free full text in PMC](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8371605/) | Protein-structure prediction and its assessment in CASP. |

John McCarthy's freely available [**What is Artificial Intelligence?**](https://www-formal.stanford.edu/jmc/whatisai/node1.html) is an additional primary source for the breadth of the ambition. Its opening questions show how broad a programme the term can describe.

In his [review of *The Question of Artificial Intelligence*](https://www-formal.stanford.edu/jmc/reviews/bloomfield/bloomfield.html), McCarthy recalls wanting to distinguish his programme from cybernetics. Search for “one of the reasons” to find the relevant paragraph. Read it as a participant's later account of his own motives, alongside the contemporary proposal.
